slides.title: Purpose and indications
bullets: A parasite is an organism that lives, for its whole life or part of its life cycle, at the expense of another organism (the host); parasites can be found in stool, blood, urine, sputum and tissues.
Medically important parasites are divided into protozoa (single-celled; not all pathogenic) and helminths (multicellular worms; always pathogenic).
In stool protozoa appear as trophozoites and cysts, helminths as eggs, larvae, adult worms or their fragments.

The test is done to find infections that cause diarrhoea, weight loss and malabsorption, chronic infections with serious complications, to tell amoebic from bacterial dysentery when stool contains blood and mucus, and to follow local infestation (for example pinworm).

slides.title: Collecting and storing the specimen
bullets: A wide-mouthed container with a tight lid is needed — clean, dry, airtight and free of disinfectant residue; paper, cardboard and matchboxes are not suitable.
About 10 mL of liquid stool is taken and examined within 15 minutes (motile parasites); formed stool within 1 hour (Aripova: 2 g; the rural-clinic manual: a teaspoon).
A specimen that is too small, or mixed with urine or dirt, is not accepted: urine destroys amoebic trophozoites and dirt interferes with microscopy.
For parasites shed intermittently (for example G. lamblia) several specimens on alternate days may be needed.
The request form gives the patient’s name, the date and, if possible, the time of collection.
If the specimen cannot be examined at once it may be kept for a few hours in a refrigerator or the coolest place in the laboratory, but it is analysed the same day; protect it from sun and heat.

slides.title: Macroscopic examination
bullets: 1. Check that the label details match the request form; open specimens one at a time.
2. Note colour, consistency and the presence of blood, mucus, pus, worms, tapeworm segments or adult pinworms.
3. Close the container; move to the next specimen or prepare the wet mount at once.
4. When many specimens arrive, examine those with blood and mucus first (for dysentery amoeba), then watery stool — motile trophozoites are found there.
5. Record the results; normal stool is formed, dark brown, and free of blood, mucus, pus and worms.

slides.title: Wet mount from watery stool (with eosin)
bullets: 1. Number the specimen and the slide with the same number.

2. With an applicator take a little stool containing particles of blood and pus and put it near one edge of the slide; cover with a cover glass without saline and press gently through a wipe to make it thin.
3. Put a drop of eosin at the other end — do this before stool touches the slide, so the dropper is not contaminated.
4. Mix a little more stool with the eosin and lower the cover glass, held by a corner, without air bubbles.
5. Examine at once: if the slide dries, trophozoites and flagellates lose their motility.
6. Eosin does not stain living trophozoites — it gives a pink background that makes them easier to see.

slides.title: Wet mount from formed stool (saline and iodine)
bullets: 1. Number the specimen and the slide; put a drop of 0.85% saline on one half of the slide and a drop of 2% iodine on the other, before any stool touches it.
2. Mix the stool with an applicator so that any parasites are spread evenly.
3. Mix a match-head-sized piece first with saline, then another piece of the same specimen with iodine.
4. Make a thin, even smear: printed text should be readable through it; a smear that is too thick or too thin makes diagnosis difficult.
5. Cover each with a cover glass without air bubbles and examine at once, before they dry.

slides.title: Microscopy
bullets: 1. View the slide with the 10× objective and the condenser sufficiently closed (too much light lowers contrast); examine the whole slide systematically, moving it forward and back or up and down.
2. Look for motile trophozoites, flagellates, helminth eggs, larvae and cysts.
3. To identify colourless parasites set the condenser for more contrast and change to the 40× objective.
4. Before reporting “no parasites found” examine several fields with the 40× objective.
5. In the iodine slide cysts are identified by size, shape, nuclei and number of inclusions.
6. Record and count all parasites found in the saline slide.

slides.title: Protozoa: key features
rows: Entamoeba histolytica
Moves in one direction; one nucleus with a central karyosome; ingested red cells inside — a diagnostic sign
Round, 1–4 nuclei (in the iodine slide), central karyosome
Giardia lamblia
Pear-shaped, spins quickly; sucking disc on the ventral side, two nuclei, four pairs of flagella
Small oval, four nuclei (sometimes hard to see), axostyles, remnants of flagella
Balantidium coli
Large oval, rotating movement, cilia, macronucleus; often red cells inside
Large round, thick-walled, nucleus well stained by iodine, contractile vacuoles
Isospora belli
Oval cyst (oocyst), usually with a granular zygote; iodine does not stain it (in an unstained wet mount)

slides.title: Notes on telling protozoa apart
bullets: Cysts of E. histolytica are told from cysts of non-pathogenic amoebae (E. hartmanni, E. coli, E. buetschlii, E. nana) by size, number of nuclei, and the presence of peripheral chromatin and a glycogen vacuole.

Trophozoites of non-pathogenic flagellates (Chilomastix mesnili, Trichomonas hominis, Enteromonas hominis, Retortamonas intestinalis) have one nucleus and fewer flagella; their cysts are smaller and lack flagellar remnants — this separates them from Giardia.

Cryptosporidium parvum and Cyclospora cayetanensis may be seen in a wet mount but are easier to find with the modified Ziehl–Neelsen stain; if they are suspected the patient is referred to a large laboratory.
Not all protozoa are pathogenic, so correct identification of each prevents a wrong diagnosis.

slides.title: Tapeworms (cestodes)
rows: Taenia saginata, T. solium
The eggs cannot be told apart: round-oval, thick brown radially striated shell, an embryo with 3 pairs of hooks inside. Eggs are shed irregularly, so the diagnosis is often made from segments
Hymenolepis nana
Egg oval or round, colourless or pale grey; embryo with 3 pairs of hooks, thread-like polar filaments at each end
Hymenolepis diminuta
Egg round, yellow, thick-shelled; 3 pairs of hooks, no polar filaments
Diphyllobothrium latum
Egg yellow-brown, oval; a granular mass of yolk cells around the embryo, a lid at one end (hard to see)
Dipylidium caninum
Segments look like pumpkin seeds and are motile in the specimen; eggs lie in capsules (8–15 each)

slides.title: Roundworms (nematodes)
rows: Ascaris lumbricoides
Fertilised egg round or oval, yellow, covered by a thick rough albuminous coat, granular mass in the centre
Enterobius vermicularis
Egg smooth, shell colourless, oval with one side flattened, larva inside; eggs are usually found in a perianal specimen
Trichuris trichiura
Barrel-shaped egg, a colourless plug at each pole, smooth double shell, yellow-brown, granular mass in the centre
Ancylostoma duodenale, Necator americanus
Egg oval, colourless, thin-shelled, looks divided into 4–8 cells; in stool kept longer than 12 hours a larva is visible, after 24 hours it may hatch (tell it from a Strongyloides larva)
Strongyloides stercoralis
Mainly motile larvae in stool, eggs rarely

slides.title: Flukes (trematodes)
rows: Clonorchis (Opisthorchis) sinensis, O. felineus, O. viverrini

Very small yellow-brown eggs shaped like a light bulb, smooth shell, a clear lid at the narrowed end. Hard to find in a direct wet mount — if suspected the material is concentrated by the formalin-ether method (large laboratory)
Schistosoma species

Large yellow-brown eggs; the species is told by the position of the spine: S. mansoni — lateral, S. intercalatum — terminal, S. japonicum — a small lateral knob. Intestinal schistosomiasis occurs with blood and mucus in the stool
Fasciola hepatica, F. gigantica
Large oval yellow-brown eggs, smooth shell, lid indistinct

slides.title: Concentration methods (large laboratories)
rows: Formalin-ether
Small eggs: Opisthorchis/Clonorchis, Taenia
Needs highly flammable ether or ethyl acetate; not recommended for small laboratories
Flotation in saturated sodium chloride
Eggs of Ascaris and hookworms
Cheap; usually not recommended for the eggs of other parasites
Flotation in zinc sulfate
Cysts of G. lamblia, E. histolytica; eggs of Trichuris, Opisthorchis
Zinc sulfate does not kill the parasites — take care

slides.title: Sources of error and quality control
bullets: Non-parasitic structures may be mistaken for parasites: vegetable and muscle fibres, pollen, starch cells, fat particles, yeasts, spores, soaps, hairs, fatty-acid crystals and air bubbles.
Laxatives, antacids, contrast media and some antibiotics may interfere with finding parasites.
If the slide dries or the specimen is late, motile trophozoites are not found; a parasite shed intermittently may be missed in a single specimen.
With too much light colourless eggs cannot be seen — close the condenser.
Quality depends on standardised methods and the skill of the staff: the laboratory should have positive slides or pictures against which the parasites found are compared.

slides.title: Safety
bullets: Stool specimens may contain parasites, bacteria and viruses — take the usual precautions.
Wear single-use gloves; wash the hands after work.
In concentration work zinc sulfate does not kill parasites; ether and ethyl acetate are highly flammable — work away from open flame.
Disinfect used containers, slides and instruments (according to the regulation).
